lessons.title: The Great Oceans
lessons.notes_html:
An ocean is a huge body of salt water on the Earth's surface — the largest body of water. A sea is a part of an ocean partly enclosed by land; it is a smaller body of water located on the margins of an ocean, such as the Arabian Sea and the Mediterranean Sea.

The Three Largest Oceans

  • Pacific Ocean — the largest ocean of the world, area about 166 million sq km, average depth about 4,280 m. It lies between Asia and Australia in the west and North and South America in the east, and contains the Mariana Trench, the deepest point on Earth (about 36,201 feet).
  • Atlantic Ocean — the second largest, area about 82 million sq km, average depth about 3,900 m, between the Americas in the west and Europe and Africa in the east. It is the most important and busiest trade route of the world and has the mid-oceanic ridge.
  • Indian Ocean — the third largest, area about 73 million sq km, average depth about 3,900 m, between Africa in the west, Asia in the north and Australia in the east. The Suez Canal links it with the Mediterranean Sea, making it an important trade route between the western and eastern hemispheres.

mcqs.q: Which is one of the largest oceans of the world?
mcqs.why: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean of the world, with an area of about 166 million sq km — larger than the Atlantic (82 million sq km) and the Indian Ocean (73 million sq km).

mcqs.q: The largest salt water body on the surface of the Earth is called:
mcqs.why: An ocean is the largest body of salt water on the Earth's surface. A sea is only a part of an ocean, and straits and bays are much smaller bodies of water.

mcqs.q: What is the area of the Pacific Ocean?
mcqs.why: The book gives the area of the Pacific Ocean as about 166 million sq km. The Atlantic Ocean covers about 82 million sq km and the Indian Ocean about 73 million sq km.

mcqs.q: The Mariana Trench, the deepest point on Earth, is located in:
mcqs.why: The Pacific Ocean contains the Mariana Trench, the deepest point on Earth at about 36,201 feet, as stated in the chapter's solved answers.

mcqs.q: The average depth of the Pacific Ocean is about:
mcqs.why: The book gives the average depth of the Pacific Ocean as about 4,280 m, while the Atlantic and Indian Oceans average about 3,900 m.

mcqs.q: Which is the second largest ocean of the world?
mcqs.why: The Atlantic Ocean is the second largest ocean, with an area of about 82 million sq km, lying between the Americas and Europe and Africa.

mcqs.q: The Atlantic Ocean is located between:
options: Asia and Australia in the west and the Americas in the east
Africa in the west and Australia in the east
The Americas in the west and Europe and Africa in the east
Asia in the north and Australia in the east
mcqs.why: The solved answers state that the Atlantic Ocean lies between the Americas in the west and Europe and Africa in the east. The Asia–Australia description belongs to the Pacific, and Africa–Asia–Australia to the Indian Ocean.

mcqs.q: Which ocean is linked with the Mediterranean Sea by the Suez Canal?
mcqs.why: The Suez Canal links the Indian Ocean with the Mediterranean Sea, making the Indian Ocean an important trade route between the western and eastern hemispheres.

mcqs.q: A sea differs from an ocean because a sea is:
options: A part of an ocean partly enclosed by land
The largest body of salt water on Earth
A narrow strip of water joining two seas
A big inlet of the sea into the land
mcqs.why: A sea is a part of an ocean partly enclosed by land, located on the margins of an ocean — for example the Arabian Sea. The largest salt water body is an ocean, and a big inlet of the sea is a gulf.

mcqs.q: The most important and busiest trade route of the world is:
mcqs.why: The book states that the Atlantic Ocean is the most important and busiest trade route of the world and that it has the mid-oceanic ridge.

lessons.title: Bays, Gulfs, Straits and Isthmus
lessons.notes_html:
A gulf is a large area of an ocean or sea that is partly surrounded by land — a big inlet of the sea into the land, larger than a bay. Examples are the Gulf of Mexico and the Arabian (Persian) Gulf. A bay is a part of an ocean or sea that is partly enclosed by land in a broad curve, e.g. the Bay of Bengal; it is comparatively smaller, while a gulf is larger and more deeply enclosed by land, with a narrower opening. In simple words, a gulf is a bigger bay.

Strait and Isthmus

  • Strait — a narrow strip of water which connects two large bodies of water (two seas or oceans) and separates two land masses, e.g. the Strait of Gibraltar, which connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea.
  • Isthmus — a narrow strip of land which connects two large masses of land and separates two bodies of water, e.g. the Isthmus of Panama.

Thus a strait is water and an isthmus is land — the two are opposites of each other.

mcqs.q: The Strait of Gibraltar connects:
options: The Pacific Ocean to the Indian Ocean
The Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea
The Red Sea to the Arabian Sea
The Arabian Sea to the Persian Gulf
mcqs.why: The book's solved answers state that the Strait of Gibraltar connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea and separates two land masses.

mcqs.q: A gulf is:
options: A narrow strip of water joining two seas
A narrow strip of land joining two land masses
A large area of an ocean or sea partly surrounded by land
The largest body of salt water on Earth
mcqs.why: A gulf is a big inlet of the sea into the land, partly surrounded by land — for example the Gulf of Mexico. A narrow strip of water is a strait and a narrow strip of land is an isthmus.

mcqs.q: In simple words, a gulf is:
mcqs.why: The book says a bay is comparatively smaller, while a gulf is larger and more deeply enclosed by land — in simple words, a gulf is a bigger bay.

mcqs.q: The Bay of Bengal is an example of:
mcqs.why: The Bay of Bengal is the book's example of a bay — a part of an ocean or sea partly enclosed by land in a broad curve.

mcqs.q: An isthmus is a narrow strip of:
options: Water which connects two large bodies of water
Land which connects two large masses of land
mcqs.why: An isthmus is a narrow strip of land connecting two large land masses and separating two bodies of water, e.g. the Isthmus of Panama. A narrow strip of water is a strait.

mcqs.q: The Isthmus of Panama connects:
mcqs.why: The book defines an isthmus as a narrow strip of land which connects two large masses of land and separates two bodies of water; Panama is its example.

mcqs.q: A strait separates:
mcqs.why: A strait is a narrow strip of water which connects two large bodies of water and separates two land masses — so it separates land, not water bodies.

mcqs.q: The Arabian (Persian) Gulf is an example of:
mcqs.why: The book names the Gulf of Mexico and the Arabian (Persian) Gulf as examples of a gulf — a large area of sea partly surrounded by land.

mcqs.q: A gulf differs from a bay because a gulf is:
options: Smaller and more open to the sea
Larger and more deeply enclosed by land, with a narrower opening
Completely surrounded by land on all sides
A narrow strip joining two seas
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that a gulf is larger than a bay and more deeply enclosed by land, with a narrower opening, while a bay lies in a broad curve.

mcqs.q: Which pair is correct?
mcqs.why: The chapter concludes: a strait is a narrow strip of water and an isthmus is a narrow strip of land — thus a strait is water and an isthmus is land.

lessons.title: Tides — Spring and Neap
lessons.notes_html:
The continuous rise and fall of sea level is called tides. Tides are produced by the gravitational pull of the Sun and the Moon on the Earth's oceans.

Spring Tides

When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a straight line (on the 1st and about the 15th date of the lunar month), their combined gravitational pull produces the highest high tides and the lowest low tides; these are called spring tides.

Neap Tides

When the Sun and the Moon are at right angles to each other with respect to the Earth (on about the 7th and 21st dates of the lunar month), their pulls partly cancel, producing the lowest high tides and the highest low tides; these are called neap tides.

In a classroom model, spring tides are drawn with the Earth in the centre and the Sun and Moon in one straight line with it, the water bulging most along that line; neap tides are drawn with the Sun–Earth–Moon making a right angle (90 degrees), where the bulges are smallest.

mcqs.q: The continuous rise and fall of sea level is called:
mcqs.why: The book's key answer: the continuous rise and fall of sea level is called tides. Currents are the flow of ocean water in a definite direction.

mcqs.q: The Moon, Earth and Sun are in the same plane (a straight line) on:
mcqs.why: When the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line — on the 1st and about the 15th date of the lunar month — spring tides occur. The 7th and 21st dates are the neap tide positions.

mcqs.q: Spring tides occur when:
options: The Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a straight line
The Sun and the Moon are at right angles with respect to the Earth
The Moon is hidden behind the Earth
The sea water is heated strongly by the Sun
mcqs.why: Spring tides happen when the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line, so their combined gravitational pull produces the highest high tides and lowest low tides.

mcqs.q: Spring tides produce:
options: The lowest high tides and the highest low tides
The highest high tides and the lowest low tides
Only one high tide in a month
mcqs.why: During spring tides the combined pull of the Sun and Moon gives the highest high tides and the lowest low tides. The lowest high tides and highest low tides belong to neap tides.

mcqs.q: Neap tides occur on about the:
options: 1st and 15th dates of the lunar month
5th and 25th dates of the lunar month
7th and 21st dates of the lunar month
10th and 20th dates of the lunar month
mcqs.why: Neap tides occur on about the 7th and 21st dates of the lunar month, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles with respect to the Earth. The 1st and 15th dates give spring tides.

mcqs.q: During neap tides, the Sun and the Moon are:
options: In a straight line with the Earth
On the same side of the Earth
At right angles to each other with respect to the Earth
mcqs.why: In neap tides the Sun and Moon stand at right angles with respect to the Earth, so their pulls partly cancel and the tides are weakest.

mcqs.q: In neap tides, the pulls of the Sun and the Moon:
mcqs.why: The book states that at right angles the pulls of the Sun and Moon partly cancel, producing the lowest high tides and the highest low tides.

mcqs.q: Tides are produced mainly by:
options: Winds blowing over the sea surface
The gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun
mcqs.why: The solved answers explain tides through the combined gravitational pull of the Sun and the Moon on the Earth's oceans, strongest when the three bodies are in a straight line.

mcqs.q: In a model of neap tides, the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is:
mcqs.why: The book's project model draws neap tides with the Moon above and the Sun to one side so that Sun–Earth–Moon make a right angle of 90 degrees, and the bulges are smallest.

mcqs.q: Spring tides occur about:
options: Twice in a lunar month (1st and about 15th)
mcqs.why: Spring tides occur on the 1st and about the 15th date of the lunar month — twice in a month — whenever the Sun, Moon and Earth come into a straight line.

lessons.title: Ocean Currents
lessons.notes_html:
An ocean current is the regular movement or flow of ocean water in a definite direction, like a river flowing in the ocean. Currents may be warm currents or cold currents.

Causes of Ocean Currents

  • Winds — the permanent winds blowing over the ocean surface push the water in their direction; they are the main cause.
  • Differences of temperature — warm water near the equator is lighter and flows towards the poles, while cold polar water sinks and flows towards the equator.
  • Differences of salinity — water of different salt content has different density, which produces movement.
  • Rotation of the Earth — it deflects the currents, to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere.
  • Shape of the coastlines — it changes the direction of currents.

mcqs.q: An ocean current is:
options: The continuous rise and fall of sea level
A narrow strip of water joining two seas
A huge wave raised by a storm
The regular flow of ocean water in a definite direction
mcqs.why: An ocean current is the regular movement of ocean water in a definite direction, like a river flowing in the ocean. The rise and fall of sea level is the tide.

mcqs.q: An ocean current is compared in the book to:
options: A river flowing in the ocean
mcqs.why: The solved answer describes an ocean current as being like a river flowing in the ocean, moving regularly in a definite direction.

mcqs.q: Ocean currents may be:
mcqs.why: The book states that ocean currents may be warm currents or cold currents, depending on the temperature of the water that is moving.

mcqs.q: The main cause of ocean currents is:
mcqs.why: The permanent winds blowing over the ocean surface push the water in their direction, and the book calls winds the main cause of ocean currents.

mcqs.q: Warm water near the equator:
options: Sinks and flows towards the equator
Is lighter and flows towards the poles
mcqs.why: Warm equatorial water is lighter and flows towards the poles, while cold polar water sinks and flows towards the equator — this is the temperature cause of currents.

mcqs.q: Cold polar water:
options: Sinks and flows towards the equator
Rises and flows towards the poles
mcqs.why: Cold polar water is heavier, so it sinks and flows towards the equator, while warm equatorial water flows towards the poles at the surface.

mcqs.q: Differences of salinity produce currents because:
options: Water of different salt content has different density
mcqs.why: The book explains that water of different salt content has different density, and this difference of density produces movement in ocean water.

mcqs.q: The rotation of the Earth deflects ocean currents:
options: To the left in the northern hemisphere and to the right in the southern hemisphere
To the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere
Towards the equator in both hemispheres
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that the Earth's rotation deflects currents to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere.

mcqs.q: Which of these also changes the direction of ocean currents?
mcqs.why: The book lists the shape of the coastlines as a cause that changes the direction of currents, along with winds, temperature, salinity and the Earth's rotation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT listed in the book as a cause of ocean currents?
options: The gravitational pull of the Moon
mcqs.why: The book lists five causes of currents: winds, temperature differences, salinity differences, Earth's rotation and coastline shape. The Moon's gravitational pull is the cause of tides, not of currents.

lessons.title: Importance of Oceans and Marine Biodiversity
lessons.notes_html:
Oceans are very important for life on Earth: they cover 71% of the Earth's surface and hold 97% of all its water. They strongly influence the weather and climate of the Earth and stabilize the temperature on land, produce more oxygen than the rainforests through marine plants (phytoplankton), provide the cheapest means of transport and trade between continents through sea routes and canals like Panama and Suez, contain valuable minerals, salt, oil and gas, and their tides and waves can be used to generate electricity.

Oceans as a Source of Food

Fishes like salmon, tuna, cod, halibut and marlin, and other sea animals such as prawns, crabs, oysters and seaweeds are caught and eaten by people all over the world; fishing is the livelihood of millions of people living on coasts, and sea salt is also obtained from ocean water. However, until now only about 1% of mankind's food comes from the sea, so the ocean's food potential is still largely unused.

Marine Biodiversity

Marine biodiversity means the great variety of plants and animals living in the oceans — sea otters, fishes, whales, sea turtles, sharks, corals and tiny plankton. Phytoplankton produce a large share of the Earth's oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide, keeping the air clean and the climate balanced; marine organisms form food chains on which fisheries and coastal communities depend; and coral reefs protect coasts from erosion and storms and shelter countless species.

mcqs.q: Oceans cover what part of the Earth's surface?
mcqs.why: The book states that oceans cover 71% of the Earth's surface. The figure 97% is the share of all the Earth's water that the oceans hold.

mcqs.q: Oceans hold what share of all the Earth's water?
mcqs.why: Oceans hold 97% of all the Earth's water, while they cover 71% of its surface — both figures are given in the chapter's importance of oceans.

mcqs.q: The marine plants that produce more oxygen than the rainforests are:
mcqs.why: The book credits marine plants — phytoplankton — with producing more oxygen than the rainforests; they also absorb carbon dioxide and keep the climate balanced.

mcqs.q: Only about what share of mankind's food comes from the sea?
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that until now only about 1% of mankind's food comes from the sea, and much of it is fish — so the ocean's food potential is still largely unused.

mcqs.q: Sea salt is obtained from:
mcqs.why: Sea salt is obtained from ocean water; the ocean is a source of food including fish, prawns, crabs, oysters and seaweeds, besides salt.

mcqs.q: Coral reefs protect coasts from:
mcqs.why: The book states that coral reefs protect coasts from erosion and storms and shelter countless species, which is part of the role of marine biodiversity.

mcqs.q: Phytoplankton help the environment by:
mcqs.why: Phytoplankton produce a large share of the Earth's oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide, keeping the air clean and the climate balanced.

mcqs.q: Fishing is the livelihood of:
options: People living in cold polar regions
Millions of people living on coasts
mcqs.why: The book states that fishes and other sea animals are eaten all over the world and fishing is the livelihood of millions of people living on coasts.

mcqs.q: Oceans strongly influence:
options: The weather and climate of the Earth
mcqs.why: Oceans influence the weather and climate of the Earth and stabilize the temperature on land, besides providing food, transport routes and minerals.

mcqs.q: Which fish is named in the book among sea foods caught from the ocean?
mcqs.why: The book lists salmon, tuna, cod, halibut and marlin as fishes caught and eaten from the ocean. Rohu and Singhara are river (freshwater) fishes of Pakistan.

lessons.title: Threats to the Oceans and Ocean Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Threats Facing the Oceans

  • Pollution of ocean water — oil spills from ships, industrial and city waste, and plastic thrown into the sea are killing marine life.
  • Climate change / global warming — rising sea temperature melts polar ice, raises the sea level, harms coral reefs and marine biodiversity, and makes ocean water more acidic.
  • Over-fishing is another serious threat.

Saving the Oceans and Marine Biodiversity

Marine pollution can be reduced by treating city and industrial waste before releasing it, preventing oil spills through strict safety rules for ships and punishing those who discharge oil or waste at sea, reducing and recycling plastic, using fewer chemical fertilizers and pesticides on farms, and enforcing international laws. Biodiversity can be saved by stopping water pollution, avoiding over-fishing, protecting endangered species like sea turtles and dugongs, protecting coral reefs and coastal mangroves, and making protected marine areas.

Electricity from Oceans

  • Tidal energy — the rise and fall of tides runs turbines in dams (barrages) built at the mouths of rivers and bays.
  • Wave energy — the up-and-down movement of waves moves floating devices which run generators.
  • Ocean currents — underwater turbines placed in strong currents work like wind turbines.
  • Ocean thermal energy — the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water is used to produce electricity.

We care for our water resources because only 3% of the Earth's water is fresh water, and most of it is locked in glaciers, so the usable part is very small.

mcqs.q: Two major threats facing the oceans nowadays are:
options: Pollution of ocean water and climate change
mcqs.why: The book names pollution of ocean water (oil spills, waste, plastic) and climate change/global warming as the two major threats, with over-fishing as another serious threat.

mcqs.q: Climate change harms the oceans by:
mcqs.why: Rising sea temperature melts polar ice, raises sea level, harms coral reefs and marine biodiversity, and makes ocean water more acidic, according to the solved answers.

mcqs.q: Besides pollution and climate change, another serious threat to oceans is:
mcqs.why: The book adds over-fishing as another serious threat to the oceans, besides pollution and climate change.

mcqs.q: Marine pollution can be reduced by:
options: Treating city and industrial waste before releasing it
Discharging oil from ships at sea
mcqs.why: The book's ways to reduce marine pollution include treating waste before release, preventing oil spills, recycling plastic and enforcing international laws for the protection of oceans.

mcqs.q: Which endangered species are named in the book for protection?
mcqs.why: To save marine biodiversity, the book says we should protect endangered species like sea turtles and dugongs, and protect coral reefs and coastal mangroves.

mcqs.q: To save marine biodiversity, coral reefs and coastal ______ must be protected.
mcqs.why: The solved answer lists protecting coral reefs and coastal mangroves among the ways to save marine biodiversity, along with protected marine areas.

mcqs.q: Tidal energy produces electricity by using:
options: The temperature difference of ocean water
The rise and fall of tides to run turbines in barrages
mcqs.why: Tidal energy uses the rise and fall of tides to run turbines in dams (barrages) built at the mouths of rivers and bays — a clean and renewable source.

mcqs.q: Ocean thermal energy depends on:
options: The temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water
The rise and fall of tides
mcqs.why: Ocean thermal energy uses the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water to produce electricity, as explained in the book.

mcqs.q: Fresh water makes up what share of the Earth's water?
mcqs.why: Only 3% of the Earth's water is fresh water, and most of it is locked in glaciers; the oceans hold the remaining 97% as salt water.

mcqs.q: Most of the Earth's fresh water is locked in:
mcqs.why: The book states that most of the 3% fresh water is locked in glaciers, so the usable part is very small — that is why we must care for our water resources.

lessons.title: Weather, Climate and Extreme Weather
lessons.notes_html:
Climate is the condition of the atmosphere over a long period of time, while weather describes the condition of the atmosphere over a short period. The climate of a place is therefore its usual pattern of temperature, rainfall and winds observed over many years.

Extreme Weather

An extreme weather condition is a weather event that is significantly different from the average usual weather pattern of a place — for example very heavy rain and floods, severe heat waves, droughts, or powerful storms and cyclones. Such events are becoming more frequent due to climate change, and they destroy crops, homes and lives.

mcqs.q: Climate is the condition of the atmosphere over a:
mcqs.why: The book's key answer: climate is a condition of the atmosphere over a long period of time, unlike weather, which changes over a short period.

mcqs.q: Weather, in contrast to climate, describes the atmosphere over a:
mcqs.why: The book's climate question contrasts the two: climate is observed over a long period, while weather is the condition of the atmosphere over a short period.

mcqs.q: Extreme weather is:
options: A weather event significantly different from the average usual pattern
The normal weather of a place
The average rainfall of a year
mcqs.why: Extreme weather is a weather event significantly different from the average usual weather pattern of a place, such as floods, heat waves, droughts or cyclones.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of extreme weather?
mcqs.why: The book lists very heavy rain and floods, severe heat waves, droughts and powerful storms and cyclones as examples of extreme weather events.

mcqs.q: Extreme weather events are becoming more frequent due to:
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that extreme weather events are becoming more frequent due to climate change, which is driven mainly by greenhouse gases.

options: The normal climate of every place
mcqs.why: Very heavy rain and floods are named in the book as examples of extreme weather — events significantly different from the usual weather pattern.

mcqs.why: Droughts are listed in the book among extreme weather events, together with floods, severe heat waves and powerful storms and cyclones.

mcqs.q: The climate of a place is studied over:
options: A long period of many years

options: Climate describes one day; weather describes many years
Climate and weather both describe a single day
Climate describes long-term patterns; weather describes short-term conditions
Weather is never different from climate
mcqs.why: The book's own question and key separate the two: climate is a condition of the atmosphere over a long period of time, while weather concerns short periods.

mcqs.q: Extreme weather differs from average weather because it is:
options: Exactly the same as the usual pattern
Significantly different from the usual pattern of the place
mcqs.why: By the book's definition, extreme weather is significantly different from the average usual weather pattern of a place — that difference is what makes it extreme.

lessons.title: Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
The greenhouse effect is the warming of the Earth's surface and lower atmosphere caused by greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, etc.). These gases let the Sun's rays pass in but trap the heat radiated back from the Earth, just like the glass of a greenhouse. It keeps the Earth warm enough for life, but excess greenhouse gases from human activities make it stronger and cause global warming.

Global warming is the gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface and atmosphere, mainly caused by the increase of greenhouse gases due to human activities such as burning fossil fuels and cutting forests. It is the main driver of climate change, and the average temperature of the Earth's surface is increasing.

Main Causes of Climate Change

  • Burning of fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas in industries, vehicles and power generation releases carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas.
  • Greenhouse gases from human and natural sources — methane from livestock and waste, nitrous oxide from fertilizers, etc. trap heat.
  • Deforestation — cutting of forests reduces the absorption of carbon dioxide.
  • Industrialization and transport growth, which increase emissions.
  • Natural causes — changes in the Sun's energy, volcanic eruptions and natural cycles.

mcqs.q: The main cause of climate change and global warming is:
mcqs.why: The book's key answer: the main cause of climate change and global warming is greenhouse gases, which trap the heat radiated back from the Earth.

mcqs.q: The increasing surface temperature of the Earth is called:
mcqs.why: The book's key answer: increasing surface temperature is called global warming — the gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface and atmosphere.

mcqs.q: The average temperature of the Earth's surface is:
mcqs.why: The book's key answer states that the average temperature of the Earth's surface is increasing, which is the process of global warming.

mcqs.q: Greenhouse gases trap:
options: The Sun's rays before they enter
The heat radiated back from the Earth
mcqs.why: Greenhouse gases let the Sun's rays pass in but trap the heat radiated back from the Earth, just like the glass of a greenhouse, warming the surface and lower atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a greenhouse gas named in the book?
mcqs.why: The book names carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour as greenhouse gases; methane comes from livestock, rice fields and waste and traps heat in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: The greenhouse effect is useful because it keeps the Earth:
mcqs.why: The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life; the problem is that excess greenhouse gases from human activities make it stronger and cause global warming.

mcqs.q: Global warming is mainly caused by:
options: The increase of greenhouse gases due to human activities
mcqs.why: Global warming is mainly caused by the increase of greenhouse gases due to human activities such as burning fossil fuels and cutting forests, as defined in the book.

mcqs.q: Burning of fossil fuels in industries and vehicles releases mainly:
mcqs.why: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas; reducing fossil fuel use, especially coal, is essential to tackle climate change.

mcqs.q: Deforestation worsens climate change because it:
options: Reduces the absorption of carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: Cutting forests reduces the absorption of carbon dioxide, so more of this greenhouse gas stays in the atmosphere and the greenhouse effect becomes stronger.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a natural cause of climate change named in the book?
mcqs.why: Alongside human causes, the book lists natural causes of climate change: changes in the Sun's energy, volcanic eruptions and natural cycles in the Earth's long history.

lessons.title: Threats and Effects of Climate Change
lessons.notes_html:
Two Major Threats of Climate Change

  • Rising of the sea level — caused by the melting of glaciers and polar ice — which will flood low-lying coastal areas and islands and have a severe economic impact on them.
  • Extreme weather events — more floods, droughts, heat waves and storms, which destroy crops, homes and lives.

Rising acidity of the oceans, harming coastal and marine ecosystems, is another major threat.

How Climate Change Changes Lifestyles

Hotter summers increase the use of fans, coolers and air conditioners and change clothing and working hours; uncertain rains and droughts change farming patterns, crops and food habits; floods and storms damage homes and force people to migrate; water shortages change daily routines; and new diseases spread in warmer climates. In coastal areas, rising sea level threatens homes and occupations like fishing, so people have to change the way they live and earn.

mcqs.q: Rising sea level will lead to:
mcqs.why: The book's key answer: rising sea level will lead to coastal flooding. Glacier melting is the cause of the rise; the rise itself floods low-lying coastal areas and islands.

mcqs.q: The sea level is rising mainly because of:
options: Melting of glaciers and polar ice
mcqs.why: The book states that the rising of the sea level is caused by the melting of glaciers and polar ice due to global warming.

mcqs.q: The two major threats of climate change are:
options: Rising sea level and extreme weather events
mcqs.why: The solved answer names rising sea level and extreme weather events (floods, droughts, heat waves, storms) as the two major threats of climate change.

mcqs.q: Rising acidity of the oceans harms:
mcqs.why: The book adds rising acidity of oceans as another major threat of climate change, harming coastal and marine ecosystems.

mcqs.q: Climate change changes farming patterns because of:
mcqs.why: Uncertain rains and droughts change farming patterns, crops and food habits, as explained in the book's answer on lifestyle effects of climate change.

Improving Air Quality

We can improve air quality by: reducing the burning of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) in vehicles, factories and power houses; using public transport, bicycles and electric vehicles; planting more trees, which absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen; controlling smoke and dust from industries with filters; and shifting to clean renewable energy like solar and wind power.

Why We Care About Ozone Depletion

The ozone layer in the upper atmosphere protects us by absorbing the harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays of the Sun. Its depletion (thinning, caused by gases like CFCs) lets more UV rays reach the Earth, which cause skin cancer, eye diseases (cataract), weak immunity in humans, and harm to crops and marine life. That is why we care about ozone depletion and must stop using the chemicals that destroy the ozone layer.

Every individual, society and government has to play its part.

Renewable Energy and Greenhouse Gases

Renewable energy sources — solar, wind, water (hydel) and biogas — produce electricity and heat without burning fossil fuels, so they release little or no carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. If we replace coal and oil power plants with solar panels and wind turbines, run vehicles on electricity from clean sources, and use solar energy for cooking and heating, the emission of greenhouse gases will fall greatly and global warming will slow down.

lessons.title: Climate and Human Life
lessons.notes_html:
Karachi and New York City

Karachi has a hot, dry (arid to semi-arid) coastal climate: summers are very hot, winters are mild and short, rainfall is low and uncertain, and being on the Arabian Sea coast its temperature is moderated by sea breezes; it never snows. New York City has a temperate climate with four clear seasons: summers are warm, winters are cold with snowfall, rainfall is received in all seasons, and the temperature difference between summer and winter is large. The difference is mainly due to latitude (New York is much farther from the equator), and the continental and oceanic influences on both cities.

Life in Coastal Areas

People living in coastal areas have a lifestyle closely linked with the sea: their main occupations are fishing, trade through ports, shipping, boat making and tourism. They eat more sea food (fish, prawns). Their houses are built to face sea breezes, storms and possible flooding — often light, airy and raised. They wear light cotton clothes because the climate is warm and humid. Sea breezes keep their climate moderate — neither very hot nor very cold. However, they also face risks of cyclones, high tides and rising sea level due to climate change.

Importance of Rivers

Rivers provide innumerable ecosystem services to mankind: they supply fresh water for drinking, washing and sanitation; they irrigate farmlands and make agriculture possible (the Indus river system is the backbone of Pakistan's farming); they are used to generate hydroelectric power; they provide fish as food; they serve as means of transport and trade; they deposit fertile silt on flood plains; and they support forests, wildlife and tourism along their banks. Great civilizations of the world grew on the banks of rivers.

Causes of Air Pollution

Smoke and toxic gases from factories and power plants; exhaust of vehicles; burning of fossil fuels for cooking and heating; waste combustion and burning of crop remains; dust from construction and roads; and CFCs from sprays and old refrigerators. Toxic gases enter the atmosphere due to waste combustion.

Impacts of Air Pollution

  • It causes breathing diseases (asthma, lung problems), eye irritation and heart diseases.
  • It depletes the ozone layer, letting harmful UV rays reach us.
  • It produces acid rain and smog.
  • It increases the greenhouse effect and global warming.
  • It damages crops, buildings and biodiversity.

Reducing Air Pollution

Reduce burning of fossil fuels and shift to solar, wind and hydel energy; use public transport and well-maintained, fuel-efficient vehicles; install filters in factory chimneys; stop burning waste and crop stubble in the open; plant more trees; use clean fuels (CNG/electricity) and enforce government laws against smoke-emitting vehicles and industries.

lessons.title: Global Warming and Greenhouse Gases
lessons.notes_html:
Global warming means the gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface and atmosphere due to the increased greenhouse effect — greenhouse gases trap more heat. It is melting glaciers, raising sea level and changing the climate of the whole world.

Causes of the Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is caused by greenhouse gases in the atmosphere — carbon dioxide (from burning fossil fuels and deforestation), methane (from livestock, rice fields and waste), nitrous oxide (from fertilizers), water vapour and CFCs. These gases trap the heat of the Sun which is radiated back from the Earth's surface, warming the planet.

Causes and Impacts of Global Warming

Causes: increase of greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide from burning of fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) in industries, vehicles and power houses; deforestation, which reduces CO2 absorption; methane from livestock and waste; and gases like CFCs. Impacts: the Earth's temperature rises; glaciers and polar ice melt and sea level rises, flooding coastal areas; weather becomes extreme — more floods, droughts and heat waves; crops and water resources are affected; many species face extinction; and diseases spread to new areas.

Reducing Greenhouse Gases

Reduce the use of fossil fuels, especially coal, and adopt renewable energy (solar, wind, hydel); plant trees and stop deforestation so more CO2 is absorbed; save energy and use efficient appliances; treat industrial emissions and use cleaner transport; reduce waste and methane from landfills by recycling; and follow the international climate agreements (like the 2015 Paris Agreement signed by 196 countries) to limit global temperature rise. In the book's global warming diagram, the labels show sunlight reaching the Earth, heat reflected back, greenhouse gases trapping the heat, and vehicles, factories, sprays and burning waste adding greenhouse gases.

lessons.title: Protecting Our Planet and Biodiversity
lessons.notes_html:
Effects of Air and Water Pollution on Biodiversity

Air pollution harms biodiversity: acid rain kills fish in lakes and damages forests; toxic gases weaken plants and trees; ozone depletion exposes animals and plants to harmful UV rays; and climate change destroys the habitats of many species. Water pollution kills fish, aquatic plants and the animals that depend on them; oil spills destroy sea birds and marine life; and polluted wetlands lose their species.

Reducing Plastic Use

Use cloth or paper bags instead of plastic shopping bags; carry a reusable water bottle instead of buying bottled water; avoid plastic straws, cups and plates — use steel, glass or clay utensils; buy things with less plastic packaging; reuse plastic containers; and recycle the plastic that cannot be avoided.

Caring for Our Planet

Earth is our only home — it gives us air to breathe, water to drink, land and food to live, and a suitable climate. We can protect biodiversity by stopping pollution of air, water and land; protecting forests and natural habitats and planting more trees; not hunting or trading endangered animals; making national parks and protected areas; using natural resources carefully; and spreading awareness. Local data on pollution can be collected — for example the number of smoke-emitting vehicles, dustbins versus open garbage points, and the rise in summer temperature — and local campaigns include tree plantation drives, cleanliness weeks, anti-smog measures and plastic-bag bans.

Challenges to the Textile Industry

Shortage and high cost of electricity and gas, old machinery, competition from other countries, shortage of good quality cotton and rising cost of production. lessons.title: Urbanization, Science and Industrial Growth
lessons.notes_html:
Urbanization is the growth and development of cities when a large number of people become permanently settled in relatively small areas forming cities. The physical growth of cities is called urbanization. It usually increases with industrialization, as people migrate from villages to cities for jobs and facilities.

Science, Technology and Development

Science and technology help in development in many ways: modern machinery increases production in industries and agriculture; new technology improves the quality of goods so they can compete in international trade; information technology creates new jobs and services; technology in health and education improves human resources; alternate energy technology reduces our dependence on imported fuel; and research develops new varieties of crops and better methods of production. Countries that advance in science and technology develop faster — industrialization itself is the result of science and technology.

Impact of Industrialization

Industrialization has transformed Pakistan's economy from a purely agricultural economy towards an industrial-based economy; it increased production, exports and employment, raised incomes, developed cities (urbanization) and improved the standard of living; but it also caused pollution and pressure on energy resources. Alternate energy for industry — solar, wind and hydel power — can supply cheaper and uninterrupted electricity to factories, reduce the import bill of mineral oil and make industry more competitive.

lessons.title: Modes of Transport
lessons.notes_html:
The three main types (modes) of transport are: land transport (roads and railways), water transport (rivers and seas — ships and boats), and air transport (aeroplanes). In most countries, road transport in the form of cars and buses is most important for carrying passengers; for international trade, ocean-going ships are the major form of transport.

Characteristics of Modern Transportation

  • Land transport — roads (cars, buses, trucks: flexible, door-to-door, best for passengers and short distances) and railways (trains: carry heavy loads and many passengers cheaply over long distances on land).
  • Water transport — ships and boats: the cheapest and highly economical mode, with the largest load capacity, used for heavy and bulky goods in national and international trade, but the slowest.
  • Air transport — aeroplanes: the fastest mode, used in urgent need and for valuable/light goods; aircraft can travel practically anywhere and over any type of land, but it is the most expensive and has small load capacity.

lessons.title: Significance of Transport
lessons.notes_html:
A safe and efficient transport system is the basis of a nation's progress. It carries passengers and goods from one place to another, joins markets with farms and factories, promotes trade, industry and agriculture, creates employment, and connects all parts of the country with each other and with the world.

Transport and Economic Development

  • It brings raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets, so industry grows.
  • Farmers can sell their produce in distant markets at better prices, so agriculture develops.
  • It promotes internal and international trade and increases exports.
  • It creates large-scale employment (drivers, railway and port workers, etc.).
  • It helps in the development of backward and remote areas by connecting them with cities.
  • It increases government income through taxes and trade.

Development means the growth of agriculture, industry, trade, education and health — and all of them need movement of people and goods. Without transport, resources of one region cannot reach another and the economy cannot grow.

lessons.title: Transport System of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan's transport system includes all three modes. Roads: Pakistan has around 270,000 km of roads; the National Highway N-5 (the historic Grand Trunk — G.T. Road) and the motorways (like Lahore–Islamabad and Karachi–Hyderabad) are the most important; road transport carries most of the passengers and freight. The N-5, running from Karachi through Hyderabad, Multan, Lahore and Rawalpindi to Peshawar and Torkham, has the highest traffic density in Pakistan, as it passes through the most populated and industrial areas of Punjab and Sindh.

Railways: Pakistan Railways has a dense network in Punjab and Sindh, especially along the rivers, since tracks are easier to build on flat land; it carries heavy goods and passengers between major cities. Water transport: the seaports of Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar handle almost all the foreign trade of the country. Air transport: PIA and other airlines connect the major cities of Pakistan with each other and with the world through international airports at Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad and other cities. CPEC road projects and Gwadar Port are further improving the system.

lessons.title: Seaports and Water Transport
lessons.notes_html:
The seaports of Pakistan are: Karachi Port, Port Qasim (Muhammad bin Qasim Port) near Karachi, and Gwadar Port — a deep sea port in the Arabian Sea in the city of Gwadar, Balochistan. The seaports handle almost all the foreign trade of the country.

Role of Water Transport in Trade

Water transport is the cheapest and most economical mode with the largest load capacity. In national trade, boats and ships carry goods along rivers and between the coastal cities. In international trade, ocean-going ships are the major form of transport: almost all the heavy and bulky imports and exports of Pakistan (oil, machinery, cotton, rice, etc.) move through the seaports of Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar. Canals like Suez and Panama have shortened the sea routes and increased its importance. Transportation makes international trade possible, so it is called the backbone of international trade.

Trade Through Gwadar Port

Imports through Gwadar Port include bulk cargo such as wheat, sugar and fertilizers; coal; LPG and petroleum products; machinery and goods for CPEC projects; and transit goods for Afghanistan and Central Asia. Exports through Gwadar include fish and seafood from the Balochistan coast; dates, fruits and minerals of Balochistan; rice, textiles and other Pakistani goods; and transit trade goods of the region. Gwadar is a new deep-sea port, so its trade is growing year by year under CPEC.

lessons.title: Improving Transport in Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Ways to Improve Our Transport System

Improve and maintain roads and highways and complete motorway projects; modernize the railway with new tracks, engines and wagons so more freight moves by rail; develop and fully operate Gwadar Port and improve Karachi and Port Qasim; enforce traffic rules and vehicle fitness to reduce accidents and pollution; provide good public transport (bus/metro services) in big cities; and connect remote areas with all-weather roads.

Enhancing Rail Freight

By repairing and doubling railway tracks, adding modern powerful locomotives and high-capacity freight wagons, running scheduled freight trains on time, building dry ports and container terminals at industrial cities, computerizing booking and tracking of goods, and giving freight rates that compete with road transport — the quality and share of rail freight can be greatly enhanced.

Rural and Urban Transport; Trade Routes

Urban areas have metalled roads, buses, rickshaws, metro services, railways and airports, with heavy traffic and congestion; rural areas have fewer and often unmetalled roads, less frequent buses, and use of carts, motorcycles and pickups — transport is slower and less developed. CPEC and the historic Silk Route connect Pakistan with China and Central Asia for trade; Chaman and Torkham are the main land routes for trade with Afghanistan (and onward to Central Asia); Karachi Port and Port Qasim handle the bulk of Pakistan's sea trade; and Gwadar Port gives the shortest sea access to western China and Central Asia.

lessons.title: Economic Development and Its Indicators
lessons.notes_html:
Economic development means a (positive) change in the national income of a country over time, along with improvements in the standard of living of the people — better education, health, employment and facilities. It is measured through indicators like per capita income; per capita data are obtained by dividing the total national income by the nation's population.

Development Indicators

  • Economic indicators: national income, per capita income (per capita GNP), rate of economic growth, employment/unemployment rate, inflation rate, and energy consumption.
  • Human (social) indicators: life expectancy, literacy/education rate, health facilities, infant mortality rate and access to clean water and sanitation.

Together they are combined in measures like the Human Development Index (HDI). Economic indicators help the government and organizations like the OECD to judge whether the country is developing, compare it with other countries, make better policies, and identify problems like unemployment and inflation in time. The natural rate of unemployment is the level of unemployment consistent with sustainable economic growth.

lessons.title: Human Development Indicators and HDI
lessons.notes_html:
Main Human Development Indicators

  • Life expectancy at birth — the average number of years a person is expected to live; the life expectancy measure is considered the ultimate indicator of development.
  • Education — literacy rate and mean/expected years of schooling.
  • Standard of living — per capita income (GNI per capita).

These three are combined to form the Human Development Index (HDI); Pakistan's HDI ranking in 2021-22 was 161. Human indicators also include health facilities — availability of hospitals, doctors, clean drinking water and sanitation, and low infant and child mortality — and freedom from diseases like malaria, dengue, corona, hepatitis, tuberculosis, typhoid and dysentery, which still take a heavy toll of life in poor countries.

Improving Pakistan's HDI

By improving its three parts: (1) Health — increase life expectancy by better hospitals, vaccination, clean water and control of diseases. (2) Education — raise the literacy rate and years of schooling, especially for girls and in villages. (3) Income — increase per capita income by creating jobs, developing industry and agriculture and controlling inflation and population growth.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Development
lessons.notes_html:
Roots of Modern Technology

  • Science — 'technology' has been defined as 'the science or systematic knowledge of the industrial arts', so scientific discoveries are its first root.
  • Inventions and innovations by scientists and engineers.
  • The Industrial Revolution, which applied science to machines and production.
  • Research and development (R&D) in universities and industries.
  • Education and training of skilled manpower.

Modern miracles like organ transplantation (eye, heart, kidneys transplanted from the dead into the living) are fruits of these roots.

Role of Science in Technological Development

Science is the root of technological development. Scientific discoveries give the knowledge which engineers convert into machines, medicines and methods: in industry, science-based technology increases production and quality; in agriculture it gives new seeds and methods; in medicine it has made organ transplantation (eye, heart, kidney) and control of diseases possible; in communication and transport it has connected the whole world. Without progress in science, no country can develop modern technology or compete in the world.

lessons.title: Inflation, Unemployment and Purchasing Power
lessons.notes_html:
Inflation is the general rise in prices of goods and services over time. Due to inflation, the purchasing power of the people decreases — the same money buys less.

Role of Inflation in Development

  • The poor suffer most and poverty increases.
  • Savings lose value, so investment falls.
  • The cost of production rises and exports become expensive and less competitive.
  • Economic uncertainty slows down development projects.

A low and controlled rate of inflation may be tolerable, but high inflation is a serious obstacle to the development of a country.

Stopping Unemployment and Inflation

To stop unemployment: develop industries and agriculture, promote small and cottage industries, give technical and vocational education matching market needs, encourage investment and self-employment, and control population growth. To stop inflation: increase production of goods (especially food and energy) so supply meets demand, reduce dependence on imports, control unnecessary government spending and money supply, and check hoarding and profiteering.

lessons.title: Health Care and Development
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of Health Care in Development

  • Healthy people can work more and better, so the productivity and income of the country increase.
  • Good health care raises life expectancy, the ultimate indicator of development.
  • It reduces the burden of diseases like malaria, dengue, hepatitis, tuberculosis and typhoid which still take a heavy toll of life in developing countries.
  • Healthy children attend school regularly and learn better.
  • Less spending on curing diseases leaves more resources for development.

We care about health in development because development is for human beings, and unhealthy people cannot study, work or enjoy the fruits of development. Health decides life expectancy, working capacity and the quality of life. A nation of sick people spends its resources on treatment instead of progress. So health is both a goal and a means of development.

Rich and Poor Countries — the Gap of 'Have and Have Not'

Rich countries (the 'haves') have high per capita income, high life expectancy, high literacy and advanced education, modern industries and technology, excellent health care and low death rate from diseases, low unemployment and inflation under control, and high HDI ranking. Poor countries (the 'have nots') have low per capita income, low life expectancy, low literacy rate, dependence on agriculture with weak industry and old technology, poor health care, high unemployment and high inflation reducing purchasing power, and low HDI ranking.
